facts.statement: Phorusrhacos lived during the Early to Middle Miocene, specifically from the Burdigalian to Serravallian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early to Middle Miocene (Burdigalian to Serravallian)

facts.statement: The first fossil of Phorusrhacos was discovered in 1887 by Carlos Ameghino in the Santa Cruz Formation of Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: The first fossil attributed to the genus, an isolated fragment of the mandible (lower jaw), was discovered in 1887 by Argentine paleontologist Carlos Ameghino in sediments of the Santa Cruz Formation in Santa Cruz Province, Argentina.

facts.statement: Florentino Ameghino initially misidentified the fossil as a giant, toothless sloth and placed it in the family Phorusrhacidae.
facts.quote: Florentino initially interpreted the fossil as belonging to a giant, toothless sloth and assigned the genus to its own family, Phorusrhacidae.

facts.statement: In 1891, Francisco Moreno correctly identified the specimen as a bird rather than a mammal.
facts.quote: In 1891, however, Argentine naturalist Francisco Moreno recognized that the specimen was avian rather than mammalian.

facts.statement: Phorusrhacos stood between 1.4 and 1.9 meters tall and weighed approximately 93 kilograms.
facts.quote: Phorusrhacos is estimated to have stood 1.4-1.9 m tall and weighed around 93 kg, placing it among the largest known phorusrhacids.

facts.statement: Phorusrhacos was more lithe and built for running than similarly sized phorusrhacids like Kelenken and Devincenzia.
facts.quote: Despite its size, it was more lithe and cursorial (built for running) than the similarly sized Kelenken and Devincenzia.

facts.statement: The skull of Phorusrhacos was laterally compressed, especially when viewed from the front.
facts.quote: The skull was laterally compressed, particularly when viewed from the front.

facts.statement: Phorusrhacos had short, thick, and broad cervical vertebrae that may have strengthened its neck for powerful strikes.
facts.quote: Its cervical vertebrae were short, thick, and broad, features that may have strengthened the neck for delivering powerful strikes.

facts.statement: Phorusrhacos acted as an apex predator in Santacrucian ecosystems, likely hunting ground sloths, notoungulates, and litopterns.
facts.quote: Phorusrhacos occupied an apex predator role in these Santacrucian ecosystems, likely preying on a variety of native mammals, such as ground sloths, notoungulates, and litopterns.

facts.statement: In 1989, Luis M. Chiappe and Miguel F. Soria appealed to the ICZN to conserve the name Phororhacos and suppress Phorusrhacos.
facts.quote: In a 1989 appeal to the ICZN, Argentine researchers Luis M. Chiappe and Miguel F. Soria sought to conserve the use of Phororhacos and suppress Phorusrhacos as the generic name.

facts.statement: The ICZN Commission rejected the names Phororhacos and Phororhacosidae following a ruling.
facts.quote: After judging the ruling, the ICZN Commission voted to reject the names Phororhacos and Phororhacosidae.

facts.statement: The taxonomic history of Phorusrhacos is considered muddled due to fragmentary fossils and a lack of scientific consensus.
facts.quote: The taxonomic history of Phorusrhacos is muddled due to the fragmentary nature of fossils, few of which overlap, and little consensus between scientists.

facts.statement: The etymology of Phorusrhacos is convoluted because Ameghino did not explain the origin of the generic or specific names.
facts.quote: The etymology of Phorusrhacos is convoluted. Ameghino did not explain the etymology of the generic name Phorusrhacos or the specific name longissimus.

facts.statement: Later translations like "rag-thief" and "branch-holder" were proposed based on the mistaken assumption that the name derived from the Greek word for "branch".
facts.quote: When the original derivation was no longer understood, other translations were proposed, such as the literal translation "rag-thief" and "branch-holder" based on mistaken assumption that the name was intended to derive from the Greek rhakis, "branch".

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of P. longissimus is mandible MLP-118.
facts.quote: He chose the mandible (specimen number MLP-118) as the holotype (name-bearing) specimen of P. longissimus.

facts.statement: In 1888, Florentino Moreno reported finding fossils of large birds in Monte Hermoso, Patagonia.
facts.quote: In 1888, Moreno mentioned that fossils of large birds had been found in Monte Hermoso by these expeditions.

facts.statement: The skull of Phorusrhacos discovered by Carlos Ameghino measured 69 cm in length in the field.
facts.quote: This skull was noted to measure 69 cm in length in the field

facts.statement: Between 1896 and 1899, Princeton University students led by John Bell Hatcher conducted expeditions in Santa Cruz Province to collect fossils.
facts.quote: Between 1896 and 1899, Princeton University students, under the leadership of American paleontologist John Bell Hatcher, led a series of expeditions to the same outcrops in Santa Cruz Province.

facts.statement: In 1902, William B. Scott visited the Museo de La Plata to photograph and review phorusrhacid taxa named by Ameghino, Moreno, and Mercerat.
facts.quote: in 1902, American professor William B. Scott visited the MLP and Ameghino's collections to photograph and review the taxa named by Ameghino, Moreno, and Mercerat.

facts.statement: In 1932, Marcus Farr and William John Sinclair published a detailed description of newly discovered phorusrhacid material.
facts.quote: In 1932, Sinclair and Farr described the newly found phorusrhacid material in detail

facts.statement: An associated postcranial skeleton of a phorusrhacid (AMNH 9264) was found 10 miles north of Cape Fairweather, Santa Cruz.

facts.statement: In 1891, Carlos Ameghino named the species Tolmodus inflatus, initially believing it to be a ground sloth.
facts.quote: In 1891, Ameghino named the genus and species Tolmodus inflatus, which he believed was also a ground sloth

facts.statement: Carlos Ameghino classified Phorusrhacidae within the Ratites, a group of giant birds including ostriches, Aepyornis, and Dinornis.
facts.quote: In the same paper, Ameghino classified Phorusrhacidae within Ratites, a group of giant birds like ostriches (Struthio), Aepyornis and Dinornis.

facts.statement: Sinclair and Farr suggested that Phorusrhacidae might be a paraphyletic clade, a view later authors did not support.

facts.statement: An incomplete left humerus (YPM-PVVU 15866) is now the holotype of Dryornis hatcheri, a cathartid, after being initially assigned to Phorusrhacos.

facts.statement: Mathilde Dolgopol de Sáez believed the genus Phorusrhacos contained five valid species.
facts.quote: Dolgopol de Sáez believed the genus had five valid species: P. longissimus, P. sehuensis, P. milne-edwarsi, P. inflatus, and P. delicatus.

facts.statement: American paleontologist Pierce Brodkorb revised the taxonomy of Phorusrhacidae in 1967.
facts.quote: A 1967 paper by American paleontologist Pierce Brodkorb greatly revised the taxonomy of Phorusrhacidae.

facts.statement: Pierce Brodkorb recognized Phorusrhacos as the valid generic name and reduced the genus to a single species, P. longissimus.
facts.quote: Here, he recognized that Phorusrhacos, not Phororhacos, was the valid generic name and he reduced the genus to just P. longissimus.

facts.statement: Callornis giganteus was described by Ameghino in 1895 based on a left tarsometatarsus fragment from the Santa Cruz Formation.
facts.quote: Callornis giganteus was described by Ameghino (1895) on the basis of a fragment of the left tarsometatarsus (MLP 176) that had been found in the Santa Cruz Formation of Argentina.

facts.statement: Until a 2016 study, Callornis giganteus was considered a synonym of P. longissimus.
facts.quote: Until a comprehensive 2016 study by Buffetaut, C. giganteus was thought to be a synonym of P. longissimus.

facts.statement: Darwinornis copei was described in 1891 by Moreno and Mercerat based on leg bone fragments from the Santa Cruz Formation.
facts.quote: Darwinornis copei was described in 1891 by Moreno and Mercerat on the basis of the bottom end of a left tibia, a tarsometatarsus fragment, and unidentified fragments (MLP 20-171-173) that had been found in the Santa Cruz Formation of Argentina.

facts.statement: The consensus is that Darwinornis copei is a synonym of P. longissimus.
facts.quote: The consensus is that it is a synonym of P. longissimus.

facts.statement: Darwinornis socialis was described in 1891 by Moreno and Mercerat based on a tarsometatarsus fragment from the Santa Cruz Formation.

facts.statement: Darwinornis socialis is considered a synonym of P. longissimus.
facts.quote: It is considered a synonym of P. longissimus.

facts.statement: Brodkorb considered Darwinornis zittelli a synonym of P. longissimus in 1967, a view followed by other authors.
facts.quote: It was considered a synonym of P. longissimus by Brodkorb in 1967, an assessment that other authors have followed.

facts.statement: Liornis minor was described by Dolgopol de Sáez in 1927 based on a tibiotarsus fragment from the Santa Cruz Formation.

facts.statement: Brodkorb considered Mesembriornis quatrefragesi a synonym of P. longissimus in 1967, a view supported by other authors.
facts.quote: It was considered a synonym of P. longissimus by Brodkorb in 1967, an assessment that other authors have followed.

facts.statement: Later studies consider Mesembriornis studeri a synonym of P. longissimus.
